name: Tomas Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the hill lines out of the valley depot. Wooden poles up the mountain roads, lines through forest, farms at the end of three kilometres of wire. A lot of my day is climbing with spikes and a belt, and a lot is clearing trees off the lines with a chainsaw before the winter takes them down. My son Pieter's on the same crew now. I trained him myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real work. You can see what you did at the end of the day: the pole's standing, the line's clear, the farm has power. What wears me out is the office. Every year more forms, more rules from people who've never held a chainsaw. My daughter put some AI thing on my phone at Christmas. I've never opened it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. These computer people promise the world every few years and it comes to nothing. After church I'd tell the men it was another fad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me. I've got my few years left, the house is paid, Marta and I have savings and the bit of woodland. I'd go on as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd climb, cut, go home, go to church on Sunday. Keep putting money aside every month like my father taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, even. Things as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your daughter put an AI app on your phone. Would you open it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Why would I? If it's mostly hype, it's mostly hype. My granddaughter can play with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pieter about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, the trade's still the trade. Learn it properly, look after your gear, and you'll always have work. That's what my father told me.

S0.say: I told you so. These computer people promise the world every few years and it comes to nothing, and I'd tell the men after church it was another fad.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, with the house paid, savings and the bit of woodland behind us. I'd go on as I am.
S0.do: Carries on climbing and clearing lines as normal and goes to church on Sundays. Keeps saving every month as his father taught him.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased that things stay as they should.
S0.quote: If it's mostly hype, it's mostly hype. My granddaughter can play with it.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is rooted in family, faith and the physical trade, and this scenario confirms his view of the world. He hasn't opened the AI app his daughter installed and sees no reason to. His security is solid and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can bring their computers to the office, but the mountain's still the mountain. At work I'd say keep your heads down and do good work. I'm not on the internet, so I wouldn't say anything there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'll be gone before it matters. It's Pieter I think about. He's thirty-four, two kids. If the work shrinks, it's the young ones who get squeezed, and that's not right after he spent four years in the apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what they bring in. I'd do the minimum of whatever they make us do on the tablets. And I'd tell Pieter to make himself the best climber on the hill, because they'll always need the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for myself. For my boy and the men like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work do you think they'd change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tree survey, probably. They'd send a drone instead of us walking the line. Fine. Then they'll find out the drone can't tell a sound oak from a rotten one the way an old man with a stick can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if the young ones lost out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, first, and the government for letting them do as they please with no thought for working families. A man trains for years, he should be able to count on that. Free markets, yes, but not at the price of families.

S1.say: They can bring their computers to the office, but the mountain's still the mountain. Keep your heads down and do good work.
S1.think: I'll be gone before it matters. It's my son Pieter I think about, who's thirty-four with two kids, and it isn't right if he gets squeezed after four years of apprenticeship.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company introduces and does the minimum with any new tablet systems. Tells his son to become the best climber on the hill so he stays needed.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but for his son and men like him rather than himself.
S1.quote: They'll find out the drone can't tell a sound oak from a rotten one the way an old man with a stick can.
S1.fieldNote: He trusts experience over technology and says so with dry humour. His worry is entirely for his son and the value of an apprenticeship. He blames tech firms and a government that doesn't stand up for working families, while still backing free markets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and someone should stop it. I'd say it at work, at church, at the pub. I don't care who hears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd frighten me. Not for the money. For Pieter, for his boys, for the whole idea that you learn a trade and it carries you. If a machine can climb my hill in 2028, everything I taught him is worth nothing in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight away, take whatever package there was. I'd sit down with Marta and the children and work out how we help Pieter, maybe sell timber from the woodland to give him something to start with. I'd lean on the church, the family, people we know, not on the government. And I'd keep every penny we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. It's like watching a pole you set yourself start to lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Pieter the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, you're not alone. We'll get through it as a family. And I'd probably tell him I'm sorry, because I'm the one who put him on that hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're financially secure. Why does this hit so hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because money isn't the point. My life is the work and the family and the village. If the work goes, the village goes. The young ones leave, the church empties. I've seen it happen when the mine closed in the next valley.

S2.say: It's madness, and someone should stop it. I'd say it at work, at church and at the pub, and I don't care who hears.
S2.think: It'd frighten me, though not for the money. If a machine can climb my hill in 2028, everything I taught my son is worth nothing in two years.
S2.do: Takes whatever redundancy package is offered straight away and plans with his wife and children how to help his son, possibly by selling timber from their woodland. Leans on family and church rather than government, and saves every penny he can.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, watching something he built start to lean.
S2.quote: I'd probably tell him I'm sorry, because I'm the one who put him on that hill.
S2.fieldNote: The threat he feels is to a whole way of life, not his bank balance. He compares it to a mine closure that emptied a nearby valley. His guilt about having trained his son was the rawest moment of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say it's wrong. But I'd say, all right, we've got some years, let's keep the apprenticeships going and make sure our own get looked after first. I'd say it plain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three and done anyway. So really it's Pieter again, with five years. It's not as bad as two. But it's still his whole working life gone by forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-three, nothing different. I'd help Pieter get his heavy vehicle licence or something else practical in his spare time, paid out of our savings if needed. And I'd vote for whoever promised to protect apprenticeships and local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but it's there every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd tell Pieter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell him to learn a second thing, something with his hands that a machine won't want, maybe building or timber. Five years is enough to get a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote differently, or do anything public?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote, like always, for whoever stands up for working families and the trades. I wouldn't march. That's not me. But I'd write to our representative, which I've never done in my life.

S3.say: It's still wrong, but we've got some years, so let's keep the apprenticeships going. Make sure our own people get looked after first.
S3.think: By 2031 I'm sixty-three and done anyway, so it's Pieter again. Five years isn't as bad as two, but it's still his whole working life gone by forty.
S3.do: Keeps working until sixty-three and helps his son get a heavy vehicle licence or another practical second trade, paying from savings if needed. Votes for candidates who protect apprenticeships and writes to his representative for the first time.
S3.feel: Anxious every day, though less than in the fast scenario.
S3.quote: I wouldn't march. That's not me. But I'd write to our representative, which I've never done in my life.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time lets him imagine a plan for his son, a second trade with his hands. He'd become politically active for the first time, in a quiet way. The worry is still daily and still about the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan, if they're sensible. I'd tell the young men to save and to learn more than one thing. And I'd still say the people selling this don't care about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not mine to worry about by then. But Pieter's forty-four in 2036, and his boys are teenagers. I'd want them to have a trade a machine can't do, if there is one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-three like planned, help Pieter get a second skill over the years, and put some savings aside for the grandsons' training. I'd keep the woodland in the family, because land is land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's further off, but it's still coming for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, in the woods, cutting firewood for Marta and the neighbours. Going to church. Taking the grandsons fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your grandsons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what bothers me most. I don't know what to tell them. My father knew what to tell me. I'd tell them to work hard and look after their family, and I hope that's still enough.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for families to plan, if they're sensible. Young men should save and learn more than one thing, and the people selling this don't care about us.
S4.think: It's not mine to worry about by then. But Pieter's forty-four in 2036 and his boys are teenagers, and I'd want them to have a trade a machine can't do, if there is one.
S4.do: Works to sixty-three as planned and helps his son build a second skill over the years. Puts savings aside for his grandsons' training and keeps the woodland in the family.
S4.feel: Uneasy, because it's further off but still coming for his family.
S4.quote: My father knew what to tell me. I'd tell them to work hard and look after their family, and I hope that's still enough.
S4.fieldNote: Even with ten years, his concern is for his family line rather than himself. He admits he doesn't know what advice to give his grandsons, which unsettles him. Land and family remain his anchors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. 2028. It'd take Pieter's trade before he had time to find another. What would help is the company keeping apprentices and young men on, and paying for them to learn a second trade, not the government sending cheques.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the village. Everyone talks about jobs like they're just money. Up our valley the line crew are the volunteer firemen, the ones who clear the road after a storm, the ones in church. Take the jobs and you take all that.

headlineQuote: Up our valley the line crew are the volunteer firemen, the ones who clear the road after a storm, the ones in church.
portrait: Tomas Varga is a 58-year-old hill-line worker who climbs wooden poles with spikes and clears forest from the lines, with his son Pieter, whom he trained, on the same crew. He has never opened the AI app his daughter installed, distrusts the people selling the technology, and roots his life in family, church and his valley. Financially he is secure, with a paid-off house, savings and woodland, so his fear in every scenario is for Pieter and his grandsons. AGI by 2028 alarms him because it would make the trade he passed down worthless, and he would lean on family and church rather than government. With more time, he pins his hopes on a second trade for his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would take his son's trade before he had time to find another.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping apprentices and young workers on and paying for them to learn a second trade, rather than the government sending cheques.
